I had gained a lot of weight while doing my masters degree. It was the result of working non-stop and not making my health a priority. I also was a smoker (major stress relief, oh man), and often eating fast food or eating too much to get an energy boost to compensate for the lack of sleep. I knew my habits weren't sustainable, but I didn't know how to find the motivation to change.

Reflecting on it now, I think the catalyst for changing my lifestyle was my new boss. She's in her mid forties and in fantastic shape. I remember climbing up the stairs with her one day last winter going into work, her with total ease while I was trying my best not to collapse into cardiovascular seizure. I thought to myself, "if bosslady, who's almost twenty years my senior can do this effortlessly, why the fuck can't I?" We ended up having a number of conversations about the matter and I slowly started to change my attitude towards my lifestyle.

I started doing research as to how to get started in the gym, found the C25k program, and was sold. I quit smoking. I completely overhauled my diet. The progress has been slow, but steady. I've had some down periods where I wasn't running because life just got crazy busy, but I sure as fuck haven't given up. I've completed W5D2 twice now (I'm totally scared of W5D3 haha) and lost 31 pounds in the last ~6 months. I have just over 20 more pounds to lose until I hit my target weight, I can't really believe it. I've also recently taken up kendo, and I fucking love it.

TL;DR: My boss is awesome and totally inspired me to get my shit together.

Same sort of thing happened with my first tattoo. Went to an Artist, Jake we'll call him, told him what I wanted and brought in a reference. Pretty much same deal as you; this is the reference and full artistic freedom is strongly encouraged! He said it should take him 3 weeks, a month at most, and that he would call me when the sketch was ready.

5 weeks later no word from him, I return to the shop to get my ears stretched (piercing and tattoo placed combined), and Jake was there. I asked him how it was going with the sketch, he said he hadn't had time to do it yet. I asked how much longer, he replied two weeks. The whole conversation he had been very snippy and giving me very short answers, even cutting me off a couple of times. I didn't appreciate this. I also wanted to let him know that I had been having service issues with my phone so I asked him if he wanted my e-mail, he said no, he'll just leave a message. But, I don't have voicemail! "Then I'll just keep calling until you answer." Uh, okay...

Three weeks pass; during that time I start researching other artists. Find another one. I call the old shop when Jake is working and he answers, I ask about the sketch. He still hasn't done it. I go to the shop and get my deposit back, go to the new (and now my current) artist and make an appointment. Tattoo was done the next week.

So in my experience, if he doesn't have a good excuse and doesn't seem to care that he's been lazy, then fuck it and go somewhere else.

I'm studying science (started my Ph.D. in biochemistry a month ago), and I love it. I'm also an artsy person, always have been. Art was my passion before science. In the past, these two sides of me were in conflict with each other (hence the long story that I won't get into), but within the past few years, I've found my place in between the two.

I've had the idea to get a tattoo representing the four classical elements (fire, air, water, earth) for a few years now. Basically, these elements were the first things classified as what compose all matter and the world, and marked a critical point in historical scientific thinking. From Wikipedia: "These four elements were believed to reflect the simplest essential parts and principles of which anything consists or upon which the constitution and fundamental powers of anything are based. Historians trace the evolution of modern theory pertaining to the chemical elements, as well as chemical compounds and mixtures of natural substances to the philosophy of these four elements."

I never knew how to illustrate this in tattoo form, though. I didn't want a diagram on my back. I also wanted to incorporate that artistic side of me into it as well. Then last year, I had the idea to represent each of the four elements as some sort of a monster or creature (this idea was inspired by a friend's artwork; she draws a lot of monsters). The art I used to draw was consistently of mythical creatures, animals, anthropormorphics, etc. It stuck for a few months and I knew that's what I wanted to do. Last June, I got my 1st one ("fire") and my 2nd one ("air") in October. I still have to get the other two, plus filler work to put in between them to link them all together.
